digest.title: Material Intelligence — Weekly AI for Materials Science Digest
digest.description: An AI-generated weekly digest tracking how machine learning, generative design, and autonomous experimentation are reshaping materials science research.
digest.overview: This week's preprint crop shows AI's role in materials science skewing toward infrastructure: agentic control of physical instruments, benchmarking of learned potentials against real dynamical stability rather than just held-out accuracy, and generative-predictive pipelines for chasing rare target properties like singlet fission. Two groups independently demonstrate large-language-model agents directing lab hardware (RHEED alignment during thin-film growth, and a robot-arm/pipette platform synthesizing a metal-organic framework), both emphasizing quantitative, reproducible process recording over full autonomy claims. On the computational side, new benchmarks caution that low validation error does not guarantee stable molecular dynamics or faster self-consistent-field convergence, a useful corrective to hype around learned surrogates. All items below are preprints and have not undergone peer review; claims about performance, stability, and design success rates should be read as provisional pending independent replication.

stories.title: Open-source toolkit lets AI agents drive RHEED-guided thin-film growth
stories.summary: Researchers built an open-source hardware/software toolkit that automates reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) alignment, rocking-curve acquisition, and quantitative structural analysis during pulsed laser deposition. A Model Context Protocol server lets AI agents interpret natural-language requests to select and run analyses, with an extensible adapter interface for community-developed RHEED simulation and AI-analysis methods.
stories.whyItMatters: RHEED is one of the richest real-time probes of surface evolution during epitaxial growth, but manual operation has long been a bottleneck to closing the loop on autonomous synthesis. Making RHEED control and interpretation machine-addressable is a concrete step toward agent-directed thin-film deposition, potentially accelerating discovery of oxide, nitride, and 2D-material heterostructures.
stories.limitation: This is a preprint demonstrating toolkit capability and a single agent-driven use case on one pulsed laser deposition system; it does not yet show closed-loop optimization of film quality or generalization across deposition techniques and materials classes.

sources.title: An Open-Source Hardware and Software Toolkit to Enable Agentic RHEED-Guided Thin-Film Synthesis
sources.evidence: Reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) provides rich information about evolving surfaces during thin-film growth, but non-automated, operator-dependent alignment and fragmented analysis workflows limit its potential in fully autonomous synthesis. Here, we present an open-source hardware and software toolkit that makes RHEED control and quantitative analysis accessible to operators and artificial intelligence (AI) agents. Demonstrated on a pulsed laser deposition system, the toolkit provides programmable electron-optics control, automated beam alignment and rocking-curve acquisition, and a training-free method for crystallographic azimuthal alignment. The auto RHEED application extracts structural and growth-related observables through shared graphical and programmatic interfaces, including a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. An agent-driven demonstration shows how natural-language requests can guide the selection, configuration, and execution of quantitative analyses. An extensible adapter interface streamlines the incorporation of community-developed methods for AI analysis and RHEED simulation as they emerge, supported by Markdown implementation guides designed for AI coding agents. These capabilities support complementary descriptions of surface evolution through physical measurements and learned image representations while providing a practical route for incorporating new computational methods. Together, these tools reduce barriers to automated and agentic RHEED measurements and establish a foundation for future agentic control of thin-film synthesis guided by the evolving surface.

stories.title: LLM-driven robot platform automates and quantifies MOF synthesis
stories.summary: A team combined commercial robot arms, electric pipettes, web cameras, and an electronic balance, controlled by code generated from an AI agent based on a large language model, to automate and precisely record a two-solution synthesis of the metal-organic framework ZIF-8. The platform revealed that particle size distribution depends strongly on pipette dispensing speed, a parameter rarely controlled or logged in manual synthesis, and reproduced this dependence across repeated runs.
stories.whyItMatters: Rather than chasing full autonomy, this work targets reliable, quantitative recording of process parameters that are typically invisible in manual lab work, addressing a key bottleneck for data-driven materials development: generating high-quality, reproducible synthesis data at scale using accessible, low-cost components.
stories.limitation: Demonstrated on a single well-characterized system (ZIF-8 precipitation); broader applicability to more complex, multi-step syntheses and to materials with less forgiving reaction windows remains untested. The study is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

sources.title: Quantitative control and recording of materials-synthesis processes using an automated experimentation platform
sources.evidence: Data-driven materials development requires the collection of large amounts of high-quality materials data. Full autonomy of materials experiments is anticipated, but its technical hurdles are high and its adoption remains limited. In this study, we constructed a simple, easy-to-deploy automated experimentation platform that focuses not on full autonomy but on the reliable automation and quantitative recording of experimental processes. Specifically, commercially available instruments such as robot arms, electric pipettes, web cameras, and an electronic balance are combined, components such as fixtures are fabricated with a 3D printer, and the instruments are operated by control code generated by an AI agent based on a large language model. As a demonstration, we applied the platform to a two-solution mixing experimental system and synthesized ZIF-8, a metal-organic framework. A white suspension phase was observed in the product, and X-ray diffraction measurements confirmed that it was ZIF-8. We also found that its particle size distribution depends strongly on the solution dispensing speed of the electric pipette, which is a parameter that is difficult to control or record in manual operation. This dependence was reproduced in repeated runs, confirming the repeatability of the automated synthesis. This result is a good example showing that the control and recording of process parameters that are rarely quantified in manual work can govern the quality of materials data. All control code, CAD models, and documentation are made publicly available to encourage the spread of laboratory-scale automation of experiments.

stories.title: Benchmark shows validation accuracy doesn't predict MD stability for learned potentials
stories.summary: Comparing five graph neural network interatomic potentials (SchNet, PaiNN, NequIP, Allegro, MACE) on a chloride-passivated CdSe nanocluster, Allegro achieved the lowest force errors but this did not translate to stable molecular dynamics. NequIP ran stably for a full nanosecond without extra data, while MACE needed active-learning augmentation to stabilize, and PaiNN, Allegro, and SchNet remained unstable even after adding up to 100 extra training configurations.
stories.whyItMatters: This directly challenges the common practice of selecting machine-learning interatomic potentials purely by held-out force/energy error. For finite, surface-dominated nanostructures relevant to quantum dots and catalysts, long-timescale dynamical testing and uncertainty-guided active learning appear essential for trustworthy deployment.
stories.limitation: Findings are based on a single 149-atom CdSe nanocluster system and one thermodynamic condition (300 K, 1 ns); generalization to other nanocrystal chemistries, larger systems, or longer timescales is not established. Preprint, not yet peer reviewed.

sources.title: Benchmarking Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials for Dynamical Stability in Inorganic Semiconductor Nanocrystals: A CdSe Case Study
sources.evidence: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) enable nanosecond-scale atomistic simulations of inorganic semiconductor nanocrystals, but low errors on held-out configurations do not necessarily guarantee stable molecular dynamics. We benchmark five graph-neural-network MLIPs, SchNet, PaiNN, NequIP, Allegro and MACE, for dynamical stability in a chloride-passivated cadmium selenide nanocluster containing 149 atoms. The models were trained under harmonized conditions on 1,000 configurations and evaluated against 2,000 held-out configurations generated using density functional theory, considering force accuracy, computational efficiency, uncertainty and structural stability during 1 ns simulations at 300 K. Allegro produced the lowest validation force mean absolute errors, ranging from 12 to 14 meV per angstrom, whereas SchNet produced the largest, ranging from 84 to 110 meV per angstrom. This ranking did not predict dynamical robustness: NequIP remained stable for 1 ns without additional training data, whereas MACE became stable only after an ensemble-based active-learning procedure added 34 uncertainty-selected configurations. PaiNN and Allegro remained unstable after the addition of 100 and 95 configurations, respectively, and SchNet also failed to achieve stable dynamics within the tested augmentation budget. Under the benchmark hardware conditions, the machine-learning potentials required 6-66 ms per molecular-dynamics step, compared with approximately 20 s for density functional theory. These results show that held-out prediction errors alone are insufficient for selecting interatomic potentials for finite, surface-dominated nanostructures. Reliable deployment requires long-timescale dynamical testing combined with uncertainty-guided refinement, while the effectiveness and data efficiency of active learning remain strongly architecture dependent.

stories.title: Active-learning CALPHAD search identifies Ru-stabilized refractory BCC/B2 alloys
stories.summary: Combining CALPHAD thermodynamic calculations with random-forest-guided active learning, researchers screened a ten-element Nb-based, Ru-bearing composition space at 1 at.% resolution across 500 evaluated alloys. The approach reproduced known trends (RuHf and RuZr staying stable to the solidus) and identified 100 candidate alloys meeting criteria for high-temperature BCC+B2 dual-phase stability, including 19 previously unreported Ru-lean compositions.
stories.whyItMatters: Refractory alloys with ductile BCC matrices strengthened by ordered B2 precipitates are a high-temperature analogue to Ni-superalloy gamma/gamma-prime microstructures. Coupling active learning with CALPHAD screens a costly compositional space far more efficiently than exhaustive calculation, offering practical design rules for next-generation high-temperature structural alloys.
stories.limitation: Results are computational (CALPHAD-based) predictions of phase stability, not experimentally synthesized or mechanically tested alloys; actual processability, oxidation resistance, and mechanical performance of the flagged compositions remain unverified. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

sources.title: Machine Learning Guided CALPHAD Design of Ru-Stabilized BCC B2 Refractory Alloys
sources.evidence: Refractory alloys with a ductile body-centered-cubic (BCC) matrix strengthened by ordered B2 precipitates offer a high-temperature analogue to the gamma/gamma-prime architecture of Ni-based superalloys. Ruthenium is particularly attractive as a B2 stabilizer because RuHf, RuZr, and RuTi can retain ordered phases well above 1300 C. In this work, equilibrium CALPHAD calculations were coupled with random-forest-guided active learning to explore a ten-element Nb-based, Ru-bearing composition space containing Nb, Ta, Mo, V, Ru, Ti, Zr, Hf, Al, and Y at 1 at.% resolution. Across 500 CALPHAD-evaluated alloys, the calculations reproduced the principal trends reported for the Ru-B2 design space. RuHf and RuZr remained stable to the solidus, RuTi commonly exhibited a solutionizing window, and Al-containing alloys preferentially formed competing sigma and A15 phases. The upper bound of the BCC+B2 field increased from a median of approximately 1570 C at 5 at.% Ru to approximately 1980 C near 9-10 at.% Ru. Among the group-IV additions, Hf, Zr, and Ti produced progressively lower two-phase stability. Re-screening using physically motivated criteria identified 100 alloys satisfying requirements for high-temperature BCC+B2 stability, absence of liquid, phase purity, and appropriate secondary-phase fraction, including 19 Ru-lean compositions and two independently reported HfRu-B2 alloys. The results establish practical compositional design rules for Ru-stabilized dual-phase refractory alloys and identify phase-specific BCC/B2 lattice misfit as a key target for future design cycles.

stories.title: Generative-predictive framework raises singlet-fission molecule discovery hit rate to ~90%
stories.summary: A framework integrating a molecular structure generator, a properties predictor, and multi-criteria validation was used to search for singlet-fission (SF) chemical space, generating about 100 million candidate structures. Time-dependent DFT validation of a random 1% subset confirmed a 90.8% success rate for meeting target SF energetics, yielding a database of 283,559 candidates and an interpretable structural fragment associated with favorable SF behavior.
stories.whyItMatters: Singlet fission could help photovoltaics exceed the Shockley-Queisser efficiency limit, but SF-capable molecules are extremely rare in chemical space, making conventional virtual screening inefficient. Coupling generative design with predictive filtering demonstrates a much higher hit rate than brute-force screening for this kind of narrow, sparse target property.
stories.limitation: Success rate is based on TDDFT validation of only a 1% random subsample of generated candidates, and none of the flagged molecules have been synthesized or experimentally measured for singlet fission behavior; TDDFT itself carries known accuracy limitations for excited-state energetics. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

sources.title: Navigating Sparse Singlet Fission Chemical Space: An Intelligent Generative-Predictive Paradigm
sources.evidence: Singlet fission (SF) offers a promising route to surpass the Shockley-Queisser limit by converting a photoexcited singlet exciton into two triplet excitons, thereby enhancing photovoltaic energy conversion efficiency. However, realizing efficient SF process requires stringent energetic requirements among low-lying excited states that render SF molecules intrinsically rare within the vast chemical space. This extreme sparsity presents a grand challenge for molecular discovery. Due to low hit rates and trial-and-error computational waste on nonviable structures, conventional high-throughput virtual screening faces significant constraints, even when accelerated by machine learning models. Here, we establish a synergistic generative-predictive framework for the targeted inverse design of SF molecules by integrating a structure generator, a properties predictor and a multi-criteria validation workflow. By continuously coupling generative exploration with SF predictive models, the framework progressively enriches SF species and achieves a success rate of approximately 90% in generating molecules that satisfy the target SF energetic criteria. High-throughput evaluation of about 100 million generated structures with time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) validation of just a random 1% subset confirmed a 90.8% success rate for SF candidates. All together, we constructed an SF database of 283,559 candidates with favorable energetics of excited states and synthetic accessibility. From it, we identified a key fragment strongly associated with the requirements for SF, namely, CN([O])N(C)[O]. These findings establish an efficient route for overcoming the sparsity difficulty in SF molecular discovery and provide interpretable design principles for the development of novel excited-state functional materials.

stories.title: AIDEN neural network reconstructs real-space charge density with zero-shot transfer
stories.summary: AIDEN (Atomic-Interaction Density Equivariant Network) separates element-dependent one-center density from environment-induced redistribution, using a continuous low-rank Gaussian decoder to reconstruct charge density at arbitrary spatial coordinates. It reports state-of-the-art accuracy on periodic crystal benchmarks, competitive performance on molecules, zero-shot transfer to out-of-distribution structures, and substantially faster inference than baseline models or full self-consistent-field DFT calculations.
stories.whyItMatters: Fast, accurate surrogates for the Kohn-Sham charge density could meaningfully cut the cost of electronic-structure-driven materials screening, a persistent computational bottleneck for high-throughput computational materials design.
stories.limitation: Speed and accuracy gains are reported on benchmark datasets; how AIDEN's predicted densities perform when fed into downstream property calculations or real discovery pipelines, and how errors compound in that setting, is not evaluated here. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

sources.title: Neural-Network Solutions to Real-Space Charge Density and Generalization
sources.evidence: The Hohenberg-Kohn theorem establishes that, in principle, the ground state (GS) charge density contains all GS information of a many-electron system, such that all GS observables can be expressed as functionals of the GS charge density. Conventional Kohn-Sham density functional theory requires iterative solution of the self-consistent-field equations at substantial computational cost, motivating the development of deep learning surrogates for electronic structure calculations and, in turn, accelerating computer-aided materials design. Here, we propose \textbf{AIDEN}, an \underline{A}tomic-\underline{I}nteraction \underline{D}ensity \underline{E}quivariant \underline{N}etwork for solving real-space charge density. AIDEN separates the element-dependent one-center density from environment-induced density redistribution and represents the latter through complementary atom- and edge-centered tensor correlations. A continuous low-rank Gaussian decoder then reconstructs the density at arbitrary spatial coordinates while reusing atomic encodings independently of the evaluation grid. AIDEN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on periodic crystal benchmarks while remaining competitive for molecular systems, and further demonstrates zero-shot transferability across several structurally distinct out-of-distribution case studies. Furthermore, AIDEN provides substantially faster inference than both baseline models and full SCF calculations, enabling efficient charge density reconstruction for large-scale electronic structure calculations.

stories.title: Large SCF benchmark shows learned initializers don't always speed up DFT convergence
stories.summary: Using a new 43,851-crystal dataset (ρHD-43K) with aligned charge-density, Hamiltonian, and density-matrix labels, researchers tested whether learned predictions actually accelerate the self-consistent-field (SCF) loop of DFT, rather than just minimizing offline prediction error. Direct charge-density prediction accelerated about 91% of test crystals with a 1.18x SCF-loop speedup, but tested residual-density and Hamiltonian/matrix initializers did not consistently beat the standard atomic-density-superposition baseline.
stories.whyItMatters: This is a useful reality check for the growing field of ML-accelerated DFT: it shows that a learned model's compatibility with the nonlinear SCF solver trajectory, not just its target-space accuracy, determines real-world usefulness, which should reshape how such models are evaluated going forward.
stories.limitation: Benchmark is restricted to non-magnetic crystals on a frozen test set; behavior for magnetic, strongly correlated, or larger unit-cell systems is untested, and the modest observed speedups (median 3 fewer SCF iterations) may not justify added model complexity in all workflows. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

sources.title: Evaluating Predicted Densities, Hamiltonians, and Density Matrices as Periodic SCF Initializers
sources.evidence: Learned electronic states are usually evaluated by prediction error, even though their intended use is to accelerate the self-consistent-field (SCF) loop of density functional theory (DFT). We ask whether lower offline error actually yields a better SCF initializer. We construct $ρ$HD-43K, a 43,851-crystal DFT corpus with aligned charge-density, Hamiltonian, and density-matrix labels, and extend the solver workflow to inject all three predicted states. The closed-loop benchmark compares direct converged-state prediction against residual prediction from solver-native references on a frozen test set of non-magnetic crystals, using paired convergence, iteration, and SCF-loop timing measurements. Injecting the exact converged density matrix or Hamiltonian as an oracle upper bound cuts the median SCF count from 16 to one, revealing substantial acceleration headroom. Among learned inputs, direct charge-density prediction (Charge3Net-E3) accelerates about 91% of paired crystals, saves a median of three SCF iterations, and yields a $1.18\times$ SCF-loop speedup. In contrast, the tested residual-density and matrix initializers do not consistently improve over the standard superposition-of-atomic-densities baseline. These results establish that target-space accuracy alone is insufficient: a learned initializer must also be compatible with the nonlinear solver trajectory, and its utility must be measured in the loop.

stories.title: Physics-guided ML models prescreen point defects in SiC for quantum applications
stories.summary: Ridge, kernel ridge, and multilayer perceptron models were trained to predict defect formation energies and zero-phonon lines for point defects in 4H-SiC without requiring costly structural relaxation. For vacancies and substitutions, mean absolute errors reached 0.437 eV (formation energy) and 0.202 eV (zero-phonon line), described as useful even beyond prescreening in some cases; interstitial defects showed larger errors (1.101 eV and 0.230 eV) still deemed useful for prescreening.
stories.whyItMatters: High-throughput DFT defect screening for quantum and power-electronics applications is computationally expensive; models that skip the relaxation step could substantially widen the search space explored before committing to costly first-principles calculations.
stories.limitation: Error levels for interstitial defects are explicitly described as insufficient for detailed characterization, and the approach is validated only on 4H-SiC; transferability to other semiconductor hosts or defect chemistries is not demonstrated. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

sources.title: Prescreening Point Defects in Semiconductors With Machine Learning
sources.evidence: High-throughput calculations using density-functional theory (DFT) are commonly used to explore point defects for applications in power electronics and quantum technologies. There is currently a major shift away from these traditional simulation techniques towards machine learning (ML) methods. We explore a class of physics-guided ML models for predicting defect formation energies and zero-phonon lines (ZPL) to identify point defects for quantum applications. The models are specifically targeted for use in a prescreening step for accelerated high-throughput workflows, and are therefore designed to avoid the costly relaxation step typically present with ML interatomic potentials (MLIPs). We compare performance for single and double point defect systems in 4H-SiC with ridge, kernel ridge, and multilayer perceptron (MLP) models using three different descriptors representing the defect systems. For vacancies and substitutions, the optimized models give mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 0.437 eV for the formation energy and 0.202 eV for ZPLs, which is just above the level at which such predictions can be useful even beyond the targeted prescreening, i.e., in some applications they may completely replace the need for costly DFT calculations. For interstitials the MAEs are larger, 1.101 eV for the formation energy and 0.230 eV for the ZPL, which, while still useful for prescreening, will not generally be useful for more detailed characterization. Hence, while the results may be further improved by model design and optimization, the models presented in this work are already useful for prescreening in high-throughput characterization of point defects.
